headline: Aoris articulates a contrarian investment thesis: competition, far from being purely a threat, can make high-quality businesses more durable and mitigate the risk of competitive fade.
reasoning: Conventional analysis treats competitive moats as the primary source of business quality, but Aoris argues this framing is incomplete. Businesses that are genuinely insulated from competition face a subtler but equally dangerous risk: complacency. Without the discipline imposed by competitive markets, management can drift towards maintaining the status quo, cutting corners on service and efficiency, and failing to invest in the future. The costs of complacency are often hidden in financial metrics for years, only becoming apparent when a structural disruption — a new technology, regulatory change or substitute — exposes the underlying weakness. Conversely, businesses that win in competitive markets demonstrate that their strengths are durable and are continuously sharpened by the need to outperform rivals.
quote: Rather than competition always being a source of pressure, we believe that for the best businesses, competition can make them better. Conventional competitive advantages protect a business from competition. They do not protect a business from itself. The absence of real competition creates the temptation for complacency. At Aoris, we like businesses that win in competitive markets. It accentuates the strengths of a strong business and the weaknesses of a weak business.

headline: Aoris cites IBM as a case study of how dominant market position bred complacency and caused the firm to miss the cloud computing opportunity despite recognising it early.

By the time IBM sounded the alarm it was being left behind, it was too late to recover its position — illustrating how a lack of competitive pressure can undermine even a highly capable business.

Today, cloud computing is associated with Amazon, Microsoft and Google, but not IBM. IBM's dominant position protected it from competition, but it also allowed complacency to creep in. The focus of the business shifted towards improving margins and maintaining the status quo. By the time the company raised the alarm that it was being left behind by the market's shift to cloud infrastructure, it was too late.

headline: Aoris holds Accenture with high conviction, arguing market mischaracterises it as an AI loser when it is in fact an AI beneficiary
reasoning: Accenture's share price declined 28% in 2025 amid market fears that AI would automate white-collar workforces and shrink demand for IT consulting. Aoris disagrees, arguing enterprise AI adoption requires massive change management, cloud migration, data governance and workforce upskilling — precisely Accenture's expertise. AI also improves Accenture's efficiency in delivering outsourcing services, helping it win more business. In Q1 FY2026 (November quarter), new contract signings rose 10% year-on-year including 33 clients with contracts over $100 million, with AI-specific bookings doubling to 9% of the total. EPS has grown 10% p.a. over the last decade and Arnold expects a similar rate ahead. Fair value was assessed as approximately 10% higher at end-2025 than start of year, implying a widening valuation gap.
quote: Some market participants see Accenture as an AI loser because AI tools are easy to use. A point the company made to us more than once last year is that many investors believe their own experience with AI is representative of that of a large organisation. Individuals can download ChatGPT, and the same day can be using it to write software code, automate tasks, write reports and summarise text. AI for an enterprise is very different. To use AI effectively and at scale, an enterprise typically will need to move their many databases and hundreds of IT applications to the cloud. Data needs to be simplified, cleaned, connected, and properly governed. Access provisions and cyber security will need to be put in place and managed. Employees will need to be trained and upskilled and entire business processes changed. Large organisations are complex and usually find they need outside help to do all these things. This is what Accenture is good at. AI drives the need for change management in large organisations, and Accenture has expertise that helps its customers navigate this change more effectively than they can do themselves.
